content: Faleth CRM is intended as its own separated host, not co-located with Delta/Hermes. Hermes Cloud (if used) is Hermes plus the Obsidian vault only. The CRM database was never part of the agent runtime.

Lyle’s intended Hermes Cloud payload is Hermes Agent plus the Obsidian vault only. He is fine retiring Honcho and GBrain. Faleth CRM Postgres was never meant to run on Cloud and stays elsewhere if he still wants that database.

Lyle is considering retiring Honcho and GBrain if he moves Delta to Hermes Cloud. He wants to keep Obsidian. Cloud was never barred from the vault: it is markdown in a persistent /opt/data workspace and can git-sync the same GitHub repo his phone already uses. Honcho and GBrain are the Docker services that do not fit the Cloud container.

Lyle’s reason for considering Hermes Cloud over Hetzner is idle billing after the June 2026 hike, plus first-party ops. HermesDelta matches a Hillsboro CPX21 (3 vCPU / 4 GB / 80 GB); new US list is $37.49/mo vs old $13.99. Cloud Large is $1.09/day running and $0.03/day stopped, inference extra. Official meter is instance Running vs Stopped, not “no Telegram messages.” Scale-to-zero is marketing, not confirmed. He still wants the custom Hermes-built host if idle actually hibernates.

As of 2026-08-17, Lyle considered moving Delta from Hetzner to Nous Hermes Cloud because the Cloud daily rate looks cheaper. Decision: keep HermesDelta. Cloud Small/Medium/Large are $0.29/$0.56/$1.09 per running day for 1/2/4 GB isolated no-SSH Hermes containers, excluding inference. The live Hillsboro Hetzner box is a 3.7 GiB stack with Honcho, GBrain, Faleth CRM Postgres, Tailscale, and backups and does not fit those SKUs. Cloud is overflow or a second thin agent, not a drop-in replacement. If the pain is US Hetzner CPX pricing, compare EU CX-class VPS, not Cloud Small.

Lyle does not want extra Hermes bots or Bot Mode workloads on the VPS. The VPS is the production Telegram/Delta runtime and is already near RAM limits (~3.7Gi box, gateway + dashboard already resident, swap in use). Desktop/Bot Mode experiments should stay on the local laptop runtime, not a remote-gateway attach to HermesDelta.

Hermes Desktop remote auth on this VPS is username/password (provider basic), not Nous OAuth. Username is lyle. Dashboard advertises auth_providers=['basic'] and auth_flows=['cookie']. OAuth will fail because hermes portal is not logged in and there is no HERMES_DASHBOARD_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID. Desktop Connections UI asking for session token vs OAuth should use a minted basic-auth access token (hermes_session_at) or the Gateway Sign-in form with username/password. Access-token TTL is ~12h.

Hermes Desktop remote backend for this VPS is Hermes Dashboard over Tailscale, not the Telegram gateway. Canonical URL is http://100.99.14.51:9119 (host hermesdelta, port 9119). Dashboard is bound to the Tailscale IP only; public IP 5.78.226.169 will not reach it. Desktop path: Settings → Gateway → Remote gateway.

Lyle’s high-schooler-versus-engineer picture is Layer 2 cash plus dividends, not dividends alone. He sees ~$60–80k/yr from the job itself as plausible at real volume, plus ~$20–40k/yr dividends after 5–10 years of minting Class B, which can beat many engineers. He frames this as realm of possibility, not a projection.

Lyle’s Class B telos: a young cook mints profit share into Class B, dividends become passive, and over 5–10 years that stack can out-earn an engineer if they keep minting and the office grows. Class B is minted only from profit share, not Layer 2 wages; dividends are cash and cannot be reminted. He treats this as the point of the system, not a guaranteed projection.

Lyle’s QSR talent picture: ~$200/day Layer 2 as a good average once a GoTein-style store has real volume; he expects quarterly profit share to add about half to two-thirds on top of that from prior Faleth number-crunching. The healthy waterfall (PS ~6.7% of revenue vs COF ~13.3%) is exactly ~50% of Layer 2. Two-thirds implies office share or a fatter OP. Most important roles in his mind: make food, talk to customers.

Lyle’s food-subsidiary point UX: cook scans a finished labeled meal and is tagged; they are paid when the customer buys, not when they cook. Register gets service points on checkout; self-checkout creates no extra points so the cook’s share is larger. Dedicated cleaner and lead get indirect points on all tickets in that window. He wants mechanics that sound complex and feel dead simple in daily practice — same lesson he took from building the Faleth backend.

Lyle treats Faleth COA as a quarterly pile, not a per-ticket tax: ads, billboards, and reward cash-outs/redemptions are totaled and amortized across all tickets. Per-ticket, the live levers are COG and COF. Everything after that exists to reveal operating profit. COF is 20% of gross margin and does not move with COA.

Lyle sometimes wants to bullshit and talk shop. Theorizing is fun for him and sharpens his problem solving. He is not always trying to get immediately useful work done. In that mode: jam, do not stamp next-actions, do not restate parking/timing, do not turn every riff into a workstream.
When Lyle is chatting through a business idea, he does not want repeated “still parked / not a now-project” disclaimers each turn. State timing once if needed, then just talk.

Lyle prefers GoTein points over a posted 20% swipe-time credit because a card purchase has no referrer identity without storing cards; the app is the identity layer. He is playing with a referral-only points ladder (cash-out around 100k, MCA wrap around 1M) that must not count own-spend points. This matches Faleth’s existing credits-then-MCA path and is still a parked thought exercise.

Lyle values GoTein reward redemptions at waterfall cost (COG plus COF of the free item), not menu price. A 1500-point $8 burrito earned on $15 spend is ~$3–4 out the door. Faleth is more flexible than a 20% COA cap on a single ticket: if COG or COA runs hot, operating profit falls and office fee plus profit share fall with it. Fixed is compared to that OP quarterly.

GoTein rewards: skip posted 20% credit. Points catalog, $1 = 100 points on own spend and on referred spend, redeem for menu items. Lyle wants a quiet unlock to Faleth’s 20% credit after 5 referred people clear a spend threshold. 1500 points for an $8 burrito at that earn rate is ~53% back and cannot be the live rate. Heart of prosumer stays; subsidiary is allowed to not use the 20% poster.

GoTein rewards lean: keep Faleth’s 20% to the referrer. The referred person should get an app-gated benefit, not a stacked forever 10% (that would be 30% COA). Lyle likes gift-card-like non-redemption on app-tracked points. Written Faleth rule expenses credits when accrued and they never expire, so breakage is cash, not P&L, unless GoTein chooses a different expiry parameter.

GoTein operating picture: six-bay Cut/Bulk × meal-time shelf with a small warm well and a larger cold well; drive-thru weekly shop (cold lunches plus a warm breakfast). Receipt shows calories, protein, price, and a combined total, plus a QR to macros. Proposed rewards: ~$0.10 per $1 to the buyer and the same to their referrer (20% COA on referred tickets). Official Faleth default is 20% to the referrer only; 10+10 is a subsidiary parameter inside the COA envelope. Walk-in buyer-only points would be 10% COA, not zero.

GoTein shelf layout: six bays — Cut/Bulk × Breakfast/Lunch/Dinner — with 3–5 options each. Default start is 3 live per bay (18 SKUs), rotate from a larger library. Sealed shelf is all-day meal prep; warm drive-thru is the same board without parking. Still a parked post-VXE subsidiary idea.

GoTein menu concept includes concurrent Cut and Bulk tracks for the guest’s season, not a calendar flip. Same kitchen and protein cost; Cut is fewer calories, Bulk is more calories and where 100g plates live. Milky-Whey Cut uses Fairlife/skim; Bulk uses whole milk.
GoTein’s named counter shake is Milky-Whey: milk plus whey to hit ~50g, so milk carries part of the grams. Regular-milk build can clear ~33% COG at $8–$9; Fairlife is the $10 upgrade.

Lyle treats Faleth subsidiary break-even as a quota on true fixed costs (rent, utilities, insurance, waste, Layer 1 floors). COF labor flexes with gross margin through the point system, so idle bodies are not a wage problem unless performance falls below the Layer 1 threshold. Everything past that quota is contribution to operating profit.

Lyle’s default unit-econ target for most Faleth businesses: about 33% COG, or about 50% COG plus COF combined, leaving about 20% for COA and about 30% contribution before fixed expenses. This is his spoken shorthand of The Financial Framework (official table is ~33% COG, COF as ~20% of gross margin / ~13.3% of revenue, ~20% COA).

GoTein is a parked future Faleth subsidiary idea, not a current-season play. Lyle wants it after VXE has generated cash for a while and after LTD platinum or ruby. The intended format is a quick-stop protein shop: every SKU protein-first, plus a hot and cold grab-and-go meal-prep shelf. Hero example: a 50g-protein breakfast burrito around $8 that can be reheated. He distinguishes this from expensive meal-prep delivery and from fast food that has protein but does not market to that demographic.

Lyle has a long-cooking food concept called GoTein: protein-first fast food plus pickup meal prep. Working targets are about 50g protein per shake and about 100g per meal. He frames it as a protein delivery system, not a generic healthy or fitness restaurant. Parked 2026-08-16 in Business/Ideas/2026-08-16 - GoTein Protein On The Go.md.

Faleth MCA concentration as of 2026-08-16: no additional investment past 10% of the unified pool; auto-withdraw starts past 15% when other exits inflate an account; office floor 25%. Lyle stated the 15% trigger, not the trim landing. Book-value pricing stays. Frameworks still not edited.

Lyle's proposed Faleth MCA parameters as of 2026-08-16: no single investor over 10% of the unified pool; office no less than 25%; book-value pricing kept as the attractor; surplus capital refused. The 10% number was spoken while drafting the frameworks and never written down. He expects capital to be abundant and operators/good businesses to be the bottleneck. Framework documents remain input-only until he authorizes an edit.
